items.title: El Niño Then and Now
items.snippet: A 35-year satellite altimetry record lets scientists hold this year’s El Niño up against its strongest predecessors.

items.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
items.snippet: Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.

items.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
items.snippet: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works.

items.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
items.snippet: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.

items.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
items.snippet: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

items.title: Mother bats' hearts beat faster at the sound of their own babies' cries
items.snippet: A mother bat has one crucial challenge: find her own babies among hundreds of other bats in the colony. Making sure she cares for and nurses only her own offspring is important to ensuring their survival. Among Japanese house bats, mothers keep track of their pups using the babies' isolation calls.

items.title: How we mark our ballot can affect how we feel about voting. Here's why
items.snippet: Have you ever left a polling place feeling that your mark on the ballot didn't quite say what you wanted it to? Perhaps you liked two candidates but had to drop one, or backed the one who might actually win over the one you preferred.

items.title: Revamped playground design could protect children around the world from dangers of the sun
items.snippet: A new design methodology for school playgrounds is demonstrating how children can still enjoy their playtime while being protected from the harmful effects of the sun.

items.title: Ultrafast light pulses track molecular motion with three-femtosecond resolution
items.snippet: Researchers have observed a molecule in the first instants after it has absorbed light and tracked the coordinated motion of electrons and nuclei with a temporal resolution of three femtoseconds. This is the result achieved by an international research group led by the Politecnico di Milano, which has developed a new apparatus for studying ultrafast photochemical processes.

items.title: Shrinking iron films strengthens laser-driven demagnetization
items.snippet: From photos and videos to documents, vast amounts of data are stored on hard drives in large data centers. These devices use tiny magnetic regions whose orientation determines the information stored. But how could data be stored even faster in the future? One possible approach involves ultrashort laser pulses, which can alter the magnetic order of materials in an extremely short time.

items.title: Researcher tackles impact of a CMO's life events on businesses' bottom line
items.snippet: When a major company's CEO goes through a messy divorce or is arrested for drunk driving, investors often get nervous, worried that the executive's personal struggles will dent their returns. But most people hardly notice when a chief marketing officer has similar personal problems.

items.title: Global database provides a fuller picture of the elements that make up plant life
items.snippet: What, exactly, is a plant made of? Scientists have a good understanding of the essential nutrients plants need to grow. But what plants need and what they contain are not necessarily the same.

items.title: Brazil's presidential elections linked to decades of fluctuating environmental destruction—study
items.snippet: A University of Cambridge–led analysis of maps made from satellite imagery covering over three decades and seven presidents shows how the winner of Brazil's national elections since 1990 directly affected the preservation of its globally vital ecosystems.

items.title: Supramolecular assembly opens a new route to building quantum materials
items.snippet: A joint research team fabricated a two-dimensional structure that exhibits properties of both the honeycomb and Kagome lattices using organic molecules. They discovered that edge states specific to topological materials (states that exist only at the edges and are distinct from those in the interior) appear in this structure. items.title: How farming helped cause two medieval tsunamis in an Italian lake—and why the danger has returned
items.snippet: On Jan. 3, 1117, a strong earthquake shook northern Italy. A manuscript of the 12th century, kept today in the Vatican Library, recorded what came next: "The lakes also rose so much that very few of those living in the villages nearby escaped this danger."

items.title: 'Shock' of first England farmer hit by bird flu this season
items.snippet: The first farmer in England hit by bird flu this season tells of the "emotional roller coaster" of losing 32,000 hens.

A psychologist’s guide to understanding and spotting narcissism
items.snippet: Narcissistic people are often charming at the dinner party and cruel in the car ride home, which tells you they can control it. Clinical psychologist Ramani Durvasula, author of It’s Not You, has studied narcissism since long before it became a buzzword, and she argues that most of what circulates online gets it wrong.
